problem: Zero-shot object goal navigation methods need to pick frontiers in unknown environments, but prior approaches (e.g. VLFM-style value maps) rely on vision-language similarity alone and lack a way to use a vLLM's reasoning over accumulated history such as semantic maps.
motivation: Zero-shot ObjectNav without training on target environments is needed for robots in unknown buildings. A vLLM can reason over visual and semantic information, but it needs structured history (value map, semantic map, frontiers) to choose exploration targets efficiently.
key_idea: Use a vLLM to generate a cosine-similarity-based value map between explored areas and the target, then feed the value map, a semantic map and extracted frontier points back to the vLLM to select the next frontier to explore.
insight: Only the abstract is available, so no ablations can be cited. The abstract states that the approach explores efficiently, and works particularly well when semantic information comes from the simulator (ground truth) rather than from a perception module. This suggests semantic extraction quality is the main bottleneck.
method: Value map generation: the vLLM produces a value map between explored areas and the target object, using cosine similarity based on a prompt, from RGB-D observations with visual and semantic information.
Semantic map construction: a semantic map of the building is built incrementally from RGB-D observations.
Frontier extraction: movable frontier points are extracted from the explored map.
vLLM frontier selection: the value map, semantic map and frontiers act as historic information, and the vLLM chooses one frontier to explore next.

setting.backbone: visual LLM (vLLM), frozen; exact model not stated in abstract
setting.action_space: frontier selection (frontier points as navigation goals)
setting.privileged: Simulator ground-truth semantics in one setting (best-performing variant)

results: The abstract reports qualitative results only: the method shows potential to explore efficiently on one single-floor HM3D scene and one HSSD scene, excelling when using simulator semantic information. No numeric results or baselines are given in the abstract.
limitations: Evaluated on only two single-floor scenes (one HM3D, one HSSD), so evidence is small-scale.
Performance depends on semantic extraction quality, and it is best with simulator ground-truth semantics.
